meta.cite: Barton O. Oliver's mTOR Atlas (live data, not an archived version; give corpus_snapshot and source_commit). doi:10.5281/zenodo.22059963

data.mechanism: Reduced nutrient and energy availability is expected to lower mTORC1 through the amino-acid and energy arms at once: the sensors detect scarcity and AMPK detects the falling energy charge. Two studies support the arrow, and they differ a lot in strength. YIL2012 is the direct measurement: in mice on calorie restriction (60% of ad libitum intake) S6 and S6K1 phosphorylation fell in intestinal crypts and mTORC1 signalling fell in Paneth cells, forcing mTORC1 back on (Rheb induction or Tsc1 deletion) cancelled the effect of restriction, and rapamycin copied it. That is interventional, but it is one tissue in mice and it tested calorie restriction, not fasting. SOL2014 is weaker: mice fed ad libitum across 25 diets, where the macronutrient RATIO, not caloric intake, set lifespan and cardiometabolic health, and the mTOR link is a correlation between a lower protein-to-carbohydrate ratio and lower hepatic mTOR activation. So outside the intestine the supported variable is dietary protein, not calories.
data.mechanism_beginner: Eating less is expected to turn mTORC1 down, because the cell's fuel and amino-acid sensors both report scarcity. One study measured it directly: in mice kept on 40% fewer calories, mTORC1 activity dropped in the cells that form the stem-cell niche of the gut, switching it back on cancelled the effect, and the drug rapamycin copied it. That is one tissue in mice, and it tested eating less, not fasting. The second study behind this arrow let mice eat freely on 25 different diets and found that the ratio of protein to carbohydrate, not the number of calories, went with health and lifespan, and lower-protein diets went with lower mTOR activity in the liver. That one is a correlation, not a test. Whether eating less lowers mTORC1 in other organs, or in people, has not been shown here.
data.boundary: Supporting evidence is thinner than the claim's reputation. ROM2016 (two-year caloric restriction is tolerable in non-obese humans) and MAT2017 (rhesus survival) were removed as support in the 2026-09-21 audit because neither measured mTORC1; they belong to the CR-LONGEVITY edge. That left SOL2014, an ad-libitum 25-diet study whose own title states that the ratio of macronutrients, not caloric intake, dictates the outcome, and whose mTOR observation is correlative and confined to liver. Re-audit 2026-10-10: consensus was downgraded from established to emerging and the evidence kind from genetic epistasis to correlative, because neither matched what SOL2014 actually did. 2026-10-18: YIL2012 added. In mouse intestine, calorie restriction lowered mTORC1 activity in Paneth cells, and rapamycin or Paneth-cell genetics reproduced the stem-cell effect, so the corpus now has one direct mTORC1 measurement under restriction. It is a single tissue in mice, it tested calorie restriction rather than fasting, and it does not show the same in people. Outside the intestine the arrow is still an expectation from the sensor arms plus one correlation.

confidence.human_relevance_label: plausible in people, not shown directly
